title: Project Overview
description: Start with the README and CLAUDE.md to learn what Madar Dashboard is: the React 19 + Vite + TypeScript management interface for the Madar restaurant ecosystem, talking to a Rust (Actix-Web) backend and shipped both as a web app and a Tauri desktop app. These docs lock the stack (TanStack Router/Query, Zustand, Tailwind, Radix, Orval, i18next EN/AR) and set the house rules: generated API hooks only, Zod-typed forms, and every UI string translated.

title: Application Bootstrap
description: src/main.tsx is the dashboard's runtime entry. It wires the React Query client, Zustand app/auth stores, the i18n bootstrap, the theme helper and the global stylesheet, then mounts the TanStack Router using the generated route tree. Everything else in the tour hangs off the providers assembled here.
languageLesson: Vite entry files import CSS directly (import './styles/globals.css'); Vite turns that into a bundled stylesheet, so globals.css is the single source of truth for design tokens.

title: Routing with TanStack Router
description: Routing is file-based: every file under src/routes becomes a route, and routeTree.gen.ts (fan-out 60, the widest node in the graph) is regenerated from them. __root.tsx is the outermost shell, login.tsx the public gate, and _app/route.tsx the authenticated layout that guards access and hosts the sidebar and header. Feature pages are lazily referenced from thin route files, keeping routes declarative.
languageLesson: TanStack Router's pathless layout routes (folders prefixed with an underscore such as _app) wrap children in shared UI and loaders without adding a URL segment, and the generated tree gives fully typed links and search params.

title: App Shell and Navigation
description: Inside the _app layout, app-sidebar.tsx and app-header.tsx compose the persistent chrome, driven by the declarative nav config in src/config/nav.ts. The reusable sidebar primitive in components/ui handles collapse, mobile drawers and RTL mirroring, so adding a new module is mostly a nav entry plus a route file.

title: Auth, Stores and Scope
description: Global client state is small and deliberate: auth.store.ts holds the session and user (22 dependents), app.store.ts holds preferences such as language and theme, and use-scope / use-org-id resolve which organisation and branch every screen operates on. Nearly every feature page reads the current scope from these hooks, so understand them before the data layer.
languageLesson: Zustand stores are plain hooks created with create(); selectors like useAuthStore(s => s.user) subscribe to a slice so unrelated updates do not re-render the component. The persist middleware rehydrates from localStorage on boot.

title: The Data and API Layer
description: No component writes fetch calls by hand. orval.config.ts reads the backend OpenAPI spec and generates typed Axios functions, React Query hooks and Zod schemas; client.ts is the custom mutator that attaches the base URL and auth token (and swaps to the Tauri HTTP plugin on desktop), errors.ts normalises failures (73 dependents), and env.ts / constants.ts supply configuration. Regenerate with npm run generate:api whenever the backend changes.
languageLesson: Orval's 'mutator' option lets generated code call your own request function, so cross-cutting concerns (auth headers, platform-specific transport, error mapping) live in one file instead of in every hook.

title: Mocking with MSW
description: For local work and the public demo the app can run entirely against Mock Service Worker. handlers.ts registers request handlers built from the Orval-generated fakers, and public/mockServiceWorker.js is the worker Vite serves. This is how screenshots, tests and the playground stay usable without a live backend.

title: Shared UI Primitives
description: The presentation layer is shadcn-style: Radix primitives wrapped in components/ui (button.tsx alone has 122 dependents), merged with Tailwind classes through cn() in lib/utils.ts. form.tsx bridges React Hook Form and Zod so every dialog is strictly typed, and dialog.tsx is the base of nearly every create/edit flow.
languageLesson: cn() combines clsx (conditional class names) with tailwind-merge, which resolves conflicting utilities such as p-2 vs p-4 so callers can safely override variant styles.

title: App-Level Building Blocks
description: One level above the primitives sit the dashboard's own composites: page.tsx gives every screen the same header, actions and padding; data-table.tsx wraps TanStack Table with sorting, selection and export; empty-state.tsx and format.ts (80 dependents) keep loading, empty and number/date formatting consistent across modules. Recognising these makes any feature page readable at a glance.

title: Anatomy of a Feature Module
description: Now the pieces come together. menu-items-page.tsx and orders-page.tsx are typical feature screens: a route file renders them, they read scope from Step 5, call generated hooks from Step 6, and lay out the primitives from Steps 8 and 9. The dashboard home and inventory purchasing page show the same pattern applied to KPIs and multi-step workflows.
languageLesson: Query hooks such as useListOrders(orgId, params) return data, isLoading and error; keeping the query key derived from scope means switching branch automatically refetches without manual cache management.

title: Internationalisation and RTL
description: i18n/index.ts initialises i18next with the en.json and ar.json catalogues and persists the chosen language. Arabic is a first-class locale, so the layout flips to RTL and the design system is expected to mirror correctly; the CLAUDE.md rule that all strings go through useTranslation() is what makes this possible.
languageLesson: react-i18next's useTranslation() returns t(key, options) and re-renders on language change; nested JSON keys ("orders.status.paid") keep catalogues organised per module.

title: Customer-Facing Storefront
description: The repo ships two more Vite entry points beside the dashboard: src/order/main.tsx serves the public ordering storefront and src/get/main.tsx the landing/download surface. These run in the brand register rather than the product register, with public-ordering-page and storefront-shell handling menus, carts and per-org theming, and tracking-page following an order after checkout.

title: Design System and Product Intent
description: DESIGN.md documents the token system (navy for trust, warm accent for calls to action, cream for hospitality) that globals.css implements, while PRODUCT.md records the strategic intent: quiet and precise for the authenticated dashboard, bold and editorial for customer surfaces. Read these before any visual work so new screens match the register of their surface.

title: Tauri Desktop Shell
description: The same web bundle is packaged as a native desktop app. tauri.conf.json points the shell at the Vite build, capabilities/default.json whitelists the plugins the frontend may call (notably HTTP), and src-tauri/src/main.rs and lib.rs are the minimal Rust host that boots the webview. vite.config.ts carries the multi-entry build shared by web and desktop.
languageLesson: Tauri 2 uses a capabilities model: the frontend can only invoke commands and plugins explicitly granted in capabilities/*.json, so adding a plugin means updating both Cargo.toml and the capability file.

title: CI and Deployment
description: Two GitHub Actions workflows close the loop: deploy.yml builds the web bundles and publishes them to the production host, and release.yml builds and signs Tauri installers for each platform. Together with .env.production they show how the code you have toured reaches restaurants.
languageLesson: GitHub Actions matrix builds run the same job across operating systems in parallel, which is how a single release workflow produces macOS, Windows and Linux Tauri bundles.
